subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Newton's first law states that a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless:
options: A resultant force acts on it
questions.explain: A body's motion only changes when acted on by a non-zero resultant (net) force.

questions.q: A spring extends 0.040 m when a force of 8.0 N is applied. Its spring constant is:
Breaking stress is best described as:
options: The maximum stress a material can withstand before it fractures
The stress at the limit of proportionality
questions.explain: Breaking (ultimate tensile) stress is the maximum stress a material can bear before breaking.

questions.q: Efficiency of a machine is defined as:
options: Useful energy output ÷ total energy input
Total energy input ÷ useful energy output
questions.explain: Efficiency = useful output energy (or power) ÷ total input energy (or power).

questions.q: The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched spring (obeying Hooke's law) is given by:
questions.explain: Energy stored = area under the force–extension line = ½Fx = ½kx².

questions.q: An object of mass 240 g has a volume of 30 cm³. Its density is:
The impulse of a force is equal to:
questions.explain: Impulse FΔt equals the change in momentum Δp.

questions.q: According to Newton's third law, action and reaction forces:
options: Are the same type only by coincidence
Are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction on different bodies
questions.explain: Third-law pairs are equal, opposite, of the same type, and act on two different bodies.

questions.q: In which type of collision is kinetic energy conserved?
questions.explain: Kinetic energy is conserved only in perfectly elastic collisions; momentum is conserved in all of them.

questions.q: On a stress–strain graph, a material that absorbs a large amount of energy (large area under the curve) before fracture is described as:
questions.explain: A large area under the stress–strain curve means much energy absorbed before fracture, i.e. the material is tough.

questions.q: When a wire is loaded only up to its limit of proportionality and then unloaded, the loading and unloading lines on a force–extension graph:
questions.explain: Within the elastic (proportional) region, loading and unloading follow the same straight line.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ collides and sticks to a stationary 1000 kg car. Their common velocity afterwards is:
questions.explain: By momentum conservation, 1000×20 = 2000×v, so v = 10 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched material equals:
options: The gradient of the force–extension graph
The area under the force–extension graph
questions.explain: Work done in stretching, and hence energy stored, equals the area under the force–extension graph.

questions.q: On a velocity–time graph, the gradient represents:
questions.explain: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration.

questions.q: For a projectile launched on level ground, which launch angle gives the maximum range (no air resistance)?
questions.explain: Maximum horizontal range occurs at a launch angle of 45° on level ground.

questions.q: For a body in rotational equilibrium, the principle of moments states that:
options: Sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments about any point
questions.explain: In equilibrium the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment about any point.

questions.q: A ball of mass 0.20 kg falls 5.0 m from rest. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy just before impact is: (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
questions.explain: KE gained = loss in GPE = mgh = 0.20×9.8×5.0 = 9.8 J.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material but different lengths and areas are tested. The Young modulus is:
options: The same for both, since it is a property of the material
questions.explain: The Young modulus is an intrinsic material property, independent of the specimen's dimensions.

questions.q: For an object in complete equilibrium under several forces:
options: The resultant force is zero and the resultant moment is zero
The forces must all be equal
questions.explain: Equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.

questions.q: The Young modulus of a material is defined as:
questions.explain: The Young modulus E = tensile stress ÷ tensile strain.

questions.q: On a stress–strain graph, the Young modulus is given by:
options: The gradient of the initial linear (straight-line) region
questions.explain: E equals the gradient of the linear (Hooke's-law) part of the stress–strain graph.

questions.q: A spring of constant 50 N m⁻¹ is extended by 0.20 m. The elastic strain energy stored is:
A motor lifts a 50 kg load at constant speed through 10 m in 20 s. The useful power output is: (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
Why does a crumple zone reduce the force on car occupants in a crash?
options: It increases the mass of the car
It increases the change in momentum
It increases the time over which momentum changes
questions.explain: A longer contact time reduces the rate of change of momentum and hence the force (F = Δp/Δt).

questions.q: A 2.0 kg trolley accelerates at 3.0 m s⁻² under a resultant force. That force is:
A wire under a stress of 1.5 × 10⁸ Pa has a strain of 7.5 × 10⁻⁴. Its Young modulus is:
Which quantity is conserved in every collision in an isolated system?
questions.explain: Total linear momentum is always conserved when no external resultant force acts.

questions.q: A brittle material is one that:
options: Undergoes large plastic deformation before breaking
Breaks suddenly with little or no plastic deformation
questions.explain: Brittle materials (e.g. glass) fracture abruptly with negligible plastic deformation.

questions.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other. The magnitude of the resultant is:
questions.explain: For perpendicular vectors the resultant is √(3²+4²) = 5 N.

questions.q: Newton's second law is most fundamentally expressed as:
questions.explain: Force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = Δp/Δt; F = ma is the special case of constant mass.
